As vibe coding becomes more popular, the number of new apps on the App Store is skyrocketing, doubling in the first half of 2026, but downloads only grew by 2%. Here's the details.

Downloads are not keeping up with the growth of new apps on the App Store

A report published today by The New York Times cites new data from Sensor Tower that shows the number of new apps on the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, while downloads only grew by 2%:

The NYT's report also highlights two developers who have been pushing vibe-coded apps on the App Store: Marco Pérez, who is planning to leave JPMorgan next month to build apps full-time, and David Svensson, who launched 11 niche apps in the last five months and treats vibe coding as a hobby rather than a business.

Excerpts from the report:

Pérez is a Chicago-based software engineer who had never built a mobile app before. He spent five weeks during the winter tinkering with "vibe coding" AI tools to make a prototype, and then another two weeks to get the app ready for the App Store. That app, called InfoDrizzle, has done decently well, with 1,300 downloads so far and a profit of around $500. Pérez's next app did even better. In May, he shipped Stampa, a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps, in about a week. Stampa has since been downloaded 20,000 times and earned about $3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian also commented on another impact of the flood of submissions to the App Store in response to the NYT: there have been reports the App Store's review process has come under strain as a result.

Ajemian said "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," and added that Apple is "thrilled to see a new generation of developers using the latest tools to build and ship apps faster than ever before."

He also noted that regardless of whether or not an app is built using vibe coding, "all apps must meet the same high-quality, privacy, and security standards that our users have come to trust."
